items.complexity_note: estimate: N loop iterations issue N queries; a batched query needs 1-2 round-trips.
items.description: DB-API `execute()` (`cursor.execute('SELECT id, customer_id, total_cents FROM or…`) runs once per iteration of the loop at line 12. When the loop walks rows or IDs, the number of database round-trips grows with the data (the N+1 query pattern), and each round-trip pays driver and network latency.
items.suggestion: Load what the loop needs with one query before it (`WHERE id IN (...)`, `select(...).where(Model.id.in_(ids))`, `selectinload`/`joinedload`, Django `select_related`/`prefetch_related`/`in_bulk`) and look rows up in a dict; batch writes with `executemany`, bulk inserts, or a single UPDATE.
items.title: Database query inside a loop (N+1)
items.tradeoffs: One large query can return more data and use more memory; IN-lists have database limits (chunk them); batching writes changes transaction and error-reporting granularity; eager loading can over-fetch when only a few rows are used.

items.complexity_note: estimate: O(n·m) comparisons for n outer and m inner items; a dict index built once makes it O(n + m).
items.description: For every item of `warehouse_rows` (line 10) this code scans all of `catalog` looking for `row['sku'] == product.sku`. An equality match found by scanning is a join; the number of comparisons is the product of both collection sizes.
items.suggestion: Index the inner collection once by the join key, e.g. `by_key = {b.key: b for b in B}` (a dict of lists for non-unique keys), then look up `by_key.get(a.key)` in a single loop.
items.title: Nested loops matching items by equality
items.tradeoffs: Join keys must be hashable; duplicate keys need a dict of lists to keep every match; the index costs O(m) memory; result order can differ from the nested-loop order unless you preserve it explicitly.

items.complexity_note: estimate: O(n·m) comparisons for n loop iterations over a list of m items; a set/dict makes each test O(1) on average.
items.description: `product.category not in categories` runs inside a loop and scans `categories`, a list that also grows inside the loop. Membership tests on a list compare elements one by one, so each test costs time proportional to the list length and the loop as a whole can become quadratic as data grows.
items.suggestion: Build a set (or dict) once before the loop, e.g. `allowed = set(items)`, and test `x in allowed`; when the list grows inside the loop, maintain a parallel set.
items.title: List membership test inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: Set elements must be hashable; a set loses ordering and duplicates (keep the list if you need them); building it costs O(m) time and extra memory, so it only pays off when the test runs many times.

items.complexity_note: estimate: O(n² log n) total for n iterations vs O(n log n) once.
items.description: `best` grows inside the loop at line 64 and is sorted again on every iteration. Each sort is O(k log k) for the current size k, so the total work grows faster than the number of items.
items.suggestion: Sort once after the loop, or keep the collection ordered incrementally with `bisect.insort` / a `heapq` priority queue when the order is needed during the loop.
items.title: Re-sorting a growing collection inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: `heapq` only guarantees the smallest item is first (not a fully sorted list); `bisect.insort` is O(n) per insert because of list shifting but avoids repeated O(n log n) sorts; sort stability and key functions must be preserved.

items.description: `time.sleep(RATE_LIMIT_SECONDS)` sleeps the whole thread inside `async def get_product`. While it runs, the event loop thread is blocked, so other coroutines (concurrent requests, timers, heartbeats) cannot make progress until it returns.
items.suggestion: Use the async equivalent (`await asyncio.sleep`, `httpx.AsyncClient`/`aiohttp`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec`, an async DB driver or `AsyncSession`, `aiofiles`), or move the call off the event loop with `await asyncio.to_thread(func, ...)`.
items.title: Blocking call inside an async function
items.tradeoffs: Thread offloading adds thread-pool overhead and requires the code to be thread-safe; async libraries have different APIs, timeouts and exceptions; very short blocking calls (small local files) may not be worth changing.

items.description: `urllib.request.urlopen(EXCHANGE_URL.format(currency=currenc…` performs a blocking HTTP request inside `async def fetch_exchange_rate`. While it runs, the event loop thread is blocked, so other coroutines (concurrent requests, timers, heartbeats) cannot make progress until it returns.
items.suggestion: Use the async equivalent (`await asyncio.sleep`, `httpx.AsyncClient`/`aiohttp`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec`, an async DB driver or `AsyncSession`, `aiofiles`), or move the call off the event loop with `await asyncio.to_thread(func, ...)`.
items.title: Blocking call inside an async function
items.tradeoffs: Thread offloading adds thread-pool overhead and requires the code to be thread-safe; async libraries have different APIs, timeouts and exceptions; very short blocking calls (small local files) may not be worth changing.

items.complexity_note: estimate: O(n) per front operation, O(n²) over n iterations; deque makes it O(n).
items.description: `queue.pop(0)` removes/inserts at the front of a list inside a loop. Lists are contiguous arrays, so every front operation shifts all remaining elements.
items.suggestion: Use `collections.deque` and `popleft()` / `appendleft()`, which are O(1) at both ends.
items.title: List used as a queue (pop(0)/insert(0, …)) in a loop
items.tradeoffs: A deque does not support slicing and its indexing in the middle is O(n); code that relies on list-only methods (sort, slicing) must change; ordering semantics are the same.

items.complexity_note: estimate: N iterations → N sequential network round-trips.
items.description: `urllib.request.urlopen(EXCHANGE_URL.format(currency=currenc…` issues an HTTP request on every iteration of the loop at line 46, one after another. Total time grows with the number of iterations multiplied by the request latency.
items.suggestion: Use a batch endpoint if the API has one; otherwise issue the requests concurrently with a bound (`asyncio.gather` + `asyncio.Semaphore`, or a `ThreadPoolExecutor` for sync clients), reuse one client/session, and cache repeated responses.
items.title: Sequential HTTP request inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: Concurrency increases load on the remote service and can trigger rate limits; error handling, retries and result ordering get more complex; cached responses can be stale.

items.complexity_note: estimate: up to O(n²) characters copied for n appended pieces when the string is not resized in place; ''.join is O(total length).
items.description: `report` is extended with `+` on every iteration of the loop at line 16. Python strings are immutable, so each concatenation may allocate a new string and copy everything accumulated so far. CPython can sometimes resize in place (an implementation detail that requires no other references), so the real cost depends on the interpreter and the surrounding code.
items.suggestion: Collect the pieces in a list and call `''.join(parts)` once after the loop, or write them to an `io.StringIO`.
items.title: String built by repeated concatenation in a loop
items.tradeoffs: All pieces stay in memory until the join (similar peak to the final string); output is identical for str; for very few iterations the difference is negligible.

items.complexity_note: estimate: O(n·m) for n iterations over a list of m items; a dict/Counter/set lookup is O(1) on average.
items.description: `skus.count(sku)` runs inside a loop on a list; `list.count` scans the whole list on every call, so the cost of each call grows with the list length and the loop can become quadratic.
items.suggestion: Count all values once with `collections.Counter(items)` and read counts from it.
items.title: Linear list search/removal inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: Values must be hashable; the Counter is a snapshot and must be updated if the list changes; it uses extra memory proportional to the number of distinct values.

items.complexity_note: estimate: the call's cost is paid once per iteration instead of once in total.
items.description: `sorted(rules, key=lambda r: r.priority)` (copy/sort of a collection) is evaluated on every iteration of the loop at line 41, but none of its inputs change inside that loop, so every iteration after the first repeats identical work.
items.suggestion: Compute the value once before the loop and reuse it inside the loop.
items.title: Loop-invariant computation repeated every iteration
items.tradeoffs: Only valid if the inputs really do not change during the loop (including through aliases, other threads, or the file system); hoisting evaluates the expression even when the loop body never runs and moves where exceptions are raised.

items.description: `copy.deepcopy(state)` deep-copies the same outer object on every iteration of the loop at line 50. `deepcopy` walks and duplicates the entire object graph (with memo bookkeeping), so each iteration pays for the whole structure, which grows if the loop adds to it.
items.suggestion: Copy only what is mutated (a shallow `dict(x)`/`list(x)`/`copy.copy`, `dataclasses.replace`), build new objects instead of mutating copies, or copy once outside the loop if the source does not change.
items.title: copy.deepcopy inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: Shallow copies share nested objects, so mutating nested data would affect the original; only safe after checking which parts are modified.

items.description: `re.compile` is called with a constant pattern on every iteration of the loop at line 43. The `re` module caches compiled patterns, so each call is a cache lookup rather than a full compile, but the lookup, argument handling and call overhead repeat for an object that never changes.
items.suggestion: Compile the pattern once at module level (`PATTERN = re.compile(...)`) and call `PATTERN.search(...)` (or `.sub`, `.findall`, …) inside the loop.
items.title: Constant regex pattern processed inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: Module-level compilation runs at import time and keeps the compiled pattern alive for the life of the process; matching behavior is identical.

items.complexity_note: estimate: without memoization the call count can grow exponentially with the input (e.g. O(2^n)); with it, proportional to the number of distinct arguments.
items.description: `bundle_combinations` calls itself 2 times per invocation with arguments derived arithmetically from its parameters, and it has no cache. Such tree recursion typically recomputes the same subproblems many times.
items.snippet: def bundle_combinations(slots: int) -> int:
items.suggestion: Memoize with `@functools.cache` / `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=...)`, or rewrite the recursion bottom-up/iteratively.
items.title: Overlapping recursion without memoization
items.tradeoffs: All arguments must be hashable; the cache keeps every distinct argument tuple and result alive (bound it with maxsize); memoization is only correct for pure functions (same inputs, same output, no side effects); the recursion depth limit still applies.

items.description: `list(prices_by_region[region].keys())` copies the dict's keys into a new list on every iteration of the loop at line 60; the temporary list is allocated and discarded each time.
items.suggestion: Use the view or iterator directly: `for k in d`, `k in d`, `len(d)`, or `sum(1 for _ in it)` to count an iterator.
items.title: Needless list materialization inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: Copying `d.keys()` is required when the dict is modified while iterating; consuming an iterator to count it still exhausts it.

items.description: `_price_cache` is a module-level dict that functions add entries to, but nothing in this module removes entries or checks its size. If keys come from an unbounded domain (user IDs, request parameters), memory grows for the lifetime of the process.
items.snippet:
RATES_JSON = '{"base": "USD", "rates": {"EUR": 0.92, "GBP": 0.79, "KES": 129.5}, "symbols": ["EUR", "GBP", "KES"]}'

_price_cache = {}
items.suggestion: Bound the cache: `functools.lru_cache(maxsize=...)`, an LRU/TTL cache (for example `cachetools.TTLCache`), or explicit eviction when it exceeds a size.
items.title: Unbounded module-level cache
items.tradeoffs: Eviction causes recomputation on misses; TTL caches can serve stale values until they expire; caches shared between threads need locking or atomic operations.

items.description: A 8-element constant dict literal is rebuilt on every iteration of the loop at line 51; Python allocates and fills a new container each time even though the contents never change.
items.suggestion: Define the literal once outside the loop (a module-level constant; use a tuple or frozenset if it is never modified).
items.title: Large constant literal rebuilt inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: A shared constant must not be mutated by the loop body; if it is, keep the per-iteration copy (or copy the constant explicitly).

items.description: `open(Path(__file__).with_name('report_header.txt'), encodin…` opens a file while the module is being imported. Every process that imports this module (web workers, CLI commands, tests) pays this cost and inherits its failure modes before any code path needs the result.
items.snippet:
from pathlib import Path

with open(Path(__file__).with_name("report_header.txt"), encoding="utf-8") as _header_file:
items.suggestion: Defer the work until it is needed: move it into a function (optionally cached with `functools.cache`), an application startup hook/lifespan, or a lazily initialized attribute.
items.title: Heavy work at import time
items.tradeoffs: Lazy initialization moves the cost and any errors to first use (the first request may be slower); concurrent lazy init needs a lock; some frameworks expect module-level objects.

items.description: `json.loads(RATES_JSON)` is evaluated again with the same constant arguments as on line 67 in `currency_table`; both calls do the same work.
items.suggestion: Call it once and reuse the result within the function; if the result is stable across calls, compute it once at module level or cache it with `functools.cache`.
items.title: Same expensive call repeated with identical constant arguments
items.tradeoffs: Reusing the result assumes the underlying file, data, or remote resource does not change between the calls; a module-level cache can serve stale data and holds memory.

items.description: `re.search` receives a constant pattern on every iteration of the loop at line 30. CPython caches recently compiled patterns (a bounded cache), so this mostly costs a cache lookup per call; it becomes expensive only if many distinct patterns evict each other.
items.suggestion: Compile the pattern once at module level (`PATTERN = re.compile(...)`) and call `PATTERN.search(...)` (or `.sub`, `.findall`, …) inside the loop.
items.title: Constant regex pattern processed inside a loop
items.tradeoffs: Module-level compilation runs at import time and keeps the compiled pattern alive for the life of the process; matching behavior is identical.
